sample_evidence.section: Styled Unicode Text: Characters, Symbols & String Transformation
sample_evidence.excerpt: Styled Unicode text uses Unicode characters, symbols, combining marks, and other mappings to create alternative visual representations of ordinary text.
The term styled Unicode text is used here descriptively rather than as the name of a single formal Unicode category.

sample_evidence.section: Styled Unicode Text Is Not the Same as Changing a Font
sample_evidence.excerpt: The word font is often used informally for this kind of text, but a technical distinction is important.
Many familiar styled Latin and Greek letters and digits come from the Unicode Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols block and related Unicode ranges.

sample_evidence.section: Not Every Character Has a Styled Equivalent
sample_evidence.excerpt: Unicode does not provide a decorative equivalent for every character, language, script, punctuation mark, or visual style.
Unicode normalization can significantly affect styled text.
Styled Unicode overlaps technically with a separate Unicode problem: visually confusable characters.

sample_evidence.section: Transformation and Levenshtein Are Separate Operations
sample_evidence.excerpt: Levenshtein distance does not normalize text, transliterate scripts, change case, generate styled characters, or decide which Unicode representations should be considered equivalent.
Several kinds of transformation are common in Unicode-aware text systems. They solve different problems and should not be treated as interchangeable.
Unicode can represent canonically equivalent text using different code-point sequences.

sample_evidence.excerpt: When several transformations are used, their order can matter.

sample_evidence.section: Compatibility Normalization Can Collapse Styled Forms
sample_evidence.excerpt: Some presentation-oriented Unicode characters have compatibility mappings. As a result, applying NFKC or NFKD can collapse certain styled or presentation-specific distinctions into simpler character sequences.

Standard Levenshtein distance uses insertion, deletion, and substitution. When a transformation changes the sequence representation, it can also change which edit operations appear in the optimal alignment.
